name: In-office laser whitening
lead: In-office laser whitening is a professional tooth-bleaching procedure in which a peroxide gel is applied to the teeth and a light source, described by providers as a laser, LED or diode unit, is directed at it to accelerate the colour change.[1][3] People choose it to get a brighter smile in a single visit: Wikipedia reports that in-office bleaching can lighten teeth by two to seven shades, with effects lasting several months.[1] It is delivered by dental staff, with the gums protected by a barrier, and is one of several light-activated in-office options.[1]

Reviews have examined whether the light adds anything. A 2019 systematic review and network meta-analysis asked whether any light-activation protocol improves colour change when combined with an in-office gel.[2] Wikipedia's tooth-whitening article reports that light activation may not outperform high-concentration peroxide alone and that a 2015 study found no improvement and a possible rise in tissue temperature.[1]
Tooth sensitivity is the most commonly reported side effect of in-office bleaching.[1]
infobox: Hydrogen peroxide gel, roughly 25-38% in power-bleaching systems[1]
Halogen, LED, plasma arc, diode laser[1]

paras: Wikipedia describes in-office bleaching as involving a light-cured barrier on the gums and papillae, followed by a high-strength peroxide gel; power-bleaching gels contain about 25-38% hydrogen peroxide, and light exposure runs roughly 6-15 minutes.[1] Cosmetic-dentistry descriptions mention a rubber dam over the gums and an argon laser to speed the process, and one such description claims it is several times more effective than other methods without giving a source.[3] Only dental professionals may administer these products in many jurisdictions.[1]

Wikipedia states that the barrier is a light-cured material painted over the gums and papillae, that the bleaching agent is typically 25 to 38% hydrogen peroxide, that light sources are usually in the blue spectrum, and that sessions involve about 6 to 15 minutes of light exposure, with results measured against shade guides [1].

Wikipedia traces tooth whitening to Roman dentists using urine mixed with goat milk, late 17th-century barbers who filed and applied acid to teeth, an 1877 proposal for oxalic acid, and a late-1920s pyrozone (ether peroxide) rinse found to whiten teeth [1]. Peroxide gels were used on vital teeth in the 1940s and 1950s, William Klusmeier introduced custom-tray bleaching in the late 1960s, and Haywood and Heymann published support for tray bleaching in 1989, with whitening strips appearing in the late 1980s [1]. Light-activated in-office systems developed from this lineage, using halogen, LED, plasma arc and later diode laser sources [1].

Wikipedia reports that in-office bleaching often produces a change of 2 to 7 shades and can last several months, with yellow teeth responding best and grey teeth least; it also notes that a large share of the change from a one-hour treatment may rebound within a week.[1] Whether light adds benefit remains debated: the network meta-analysis was designed to compare light-activation systems against gel alone,[2] while Wikipedia cites findings that light did not improve results.[1]

Wikipedia reports that a 2012 systematic review (He and colleagues) found light can help when used properly without adding sensitivity, while improper use may increase sensitivity and may be no more effective than high-concentration peroxide alone, and that a 2015 study by Baroudi and Hassan found no improvement from light activators and suggested they could raise tissue temperature [1]. Home strips are described as lightening teeth by one or two shades over about 14 days [1].

Wikipedia reports that 67-78% of in-office patients experience sensitivity lasting roughly 4-39 days, and that high-concentration peroxide can irritate mucous membranes and burn gums if unprotected.[1] It also notes that light can raise tissue temperature.[1] Several registered trials have studied lasers or photobiomodulation as a way to reduce post-whitening sensitivity.[4][5]

Other reported effects on the same page include roughening of enamel, increased mercury release from amalgam for one to two days after carbamide peroxide, reduced bond strength of composite resins, uneven results and over-bleaching that can make teeth look translucent and brittle; 'bleachorexia' is described as a compulsive pursuit of whitening resembling body dysmorphic disorder [1]. The IARC found insufficient evidence that hydrogen peroxide is carcinogenic to humans [1].

Wikipedia reports that over 100 million Americans have brightened their teeth by some method, that Americans spent about $15 billion on whitening in 2010, and that whitening is the most promoted procedure in cosmetic dentistry [1]. Regulation differs: in the EU retail products are limited to 0.1% hydrogen peroxide and up to 6% is allowed under professional supervision, while the FDA endorses gels under 6% hydrogen peroxide [1]. In the UK the General Dental Council raised concerns in 2010 about untrained staff providing whitening [1].

A two-year split-mouth study of 48 patients compared in-office bleaching with and without light activation (35% hydrogen peroxide with a hybrid LED/diode laser) against other bleaching techniques, measuring colour change, stability and sensitivity.[6] A 2019 systematic review and network meta-analysis compared light-activation protocols used with in-office gel.[2] Registered trials include studies of laser versus chemical whitening and of lasers for whitening sensitivity.[4][5][7]

A 2024 registered trial of 64 participants studied photobiomodulation before or after tooth whitening to address sensitivity [8], and a registered trial begun in 2013 with 40 participants compared laser and chemical whitening methods [9].

card.summary: Peroxide gel on the teeth with a light or laser to speed it up; whether the light adds anything beyond the gel is still contested.
card.note: Sensitivity is common; colour can partly rebound.

quick.overview:
In-office laser whitening is a dentist-delivered bleaching treatment where a strong peroxide gel is applied and a light or laser unit is aimed at the teeth. Whitening itself is supported by studies; the extra role of the light is debated.

Wikipedia reports typical changes of 2 to 7 shades that can last months, with some rebound in the first week.
quick.mechanism: The peroxide gel breaks down stain molecules inside the tooth. Light or laser units are marketed as accelerating that reaction, though a network meta-analysis and other studies have examined whether they improve results over gel alone.
quick.risks: Sensitivity is reported by most patients in some studies, lasting days to weeks. Unprotected gums can be burned by strong gels, and heat from light is a reported concern. It is generally provided only by dental professionals.

chain: Peroxide gel is applied and activated with a light source
Stain molecules in enamel and dentine are broken down
Teeth look several shades lighter after one visit
angle.text: The procedure lightens tooth colour within a single appointment, which is why it is used before photos, events or other occasions where people want a brighter smile. Yellow teeth are described as responding best and grey teeth least.
